meta.title: Free Virtual Staging: What “Free” Actually Gets You | Stagify.ai
meta.description: Most free virtual staging is free to look at and paid to use: the render comes back watermarked, downscaled, or metered. Here’s the five-point test for whether you can publish a free render, and what Stagify’s free plan includes.

english.title: Free Virtual Staging: What “Free” Actually Gets You
english.figureAlt: A staged period living room with deep green walls, a white marble fireplace, a burnt-orange velvet sofa and tall arched windows, overlaid with a price card: a struck-through “$16 to $75 per staged photo” above a large “$0 on the free plan”, and the line “No watermark, full resolution, yours to publish”
english.body:
Search for free virtual staging and you will find a lot of it. Free tools, free trials, free tiers, free credits, no card required. What you find much less often is an answer to the only question that matters, which is not is it free but can I put this exact file on the MLS this afternoon?

Those two questions come apart more often than they should. A great many “free” tools are free to look at and paid to use: the render appears on screen in full, and then the download is watermarked, or shrunk to a preview, or locked behind the fourth credit. You have not been given a staged photo. You have been given a very good advertisement for one.

This is a guide to telling the difference. Since this is Stagify’s blog, it is also an honest account of what our own free plan does and doesn’t include. The test below works on any tool, ours included.

The three places “free” usually stops

Free tiers are not scams. They are marketing, and marketing has to convert, so nearly all of them are built with a gate somewhere. It is almost always one of three:

  • The watermark. The most common one, and the most fatal, because a logo across the sofa is not a listing photo. Sometimes it is subtle enough that people try to crop it out, which costs them the composition they were trying to sell.
  • The resolution. Quieter and easier to miss. The preview is beautiful; the download is 800 pixels wide. Portals and print both punish that, and you often do not notice until the photo is already live and soft.
  • The credit counter. Three free images, or five, or ten a month. Perfectly reasonable, but a single listing is eight to fifteen photos, so a free tier measured in single digits is a free tier that covers part of one listing, once.

There is a fourth, softer one worth naming: rights. Some free tiers grant you a licence to use the output rather than ownership of it, and a few reserve the right to use your images in their own marketing. That is usually buried in the terms rather than on the pricing page, and it is worth thirty seconds of reading before you upload a client’s property.

None of this makes a paid tool the answer either. Per-photo services are genuinely good and genuinely expensive at listing scale, and we put the arithmetic side by side in our honest comparison of virtual staging tools, and ranked the named players in the top 10 AI virtual staging sites for 2026. This piece is narrower: what to check before you trust a free render.

The five-question test

Run this against any tool, before you spend an afternoon on it. Every question has a yes-or-no answer and you can get all five in about five minutes.

  1. Does the file I download carry a watermark? Not the preview; the file itself. Download one and open it.
  2. What are its pixel dimensions? Check the actual file, not the promise. If it comes back materially smaller than what you uploaded, that is the gate.
  3. Do I own the output? Look for the words “copyright” or “commercial use” in the terms, and for any clause letting them republish your images.
  4. Can I choose the room and the style? A tool that stages a kitchen as a lounge because it guessed wrong is free in the same way a lottery ticket is cheap.
  5. Can I label the photo as virtually staged? This is the one nobody checks, and it is the one that has teeth. More on it below.
Question 5 is the one that bites. A watermark costs you a photo. An undisclosed staged photo is a compliance problem, and it belongs to the listing agent, not to whoever made the software.

What Stagify’s free plan includes

So, our own answers. The free plan is not a trial with a timer on it; it is a plan.

  • Unlimited free staging generations. No credit counter, no monthly allowance to ration across listings.
  • No watermark, ever, on any plan. The file you download is the file you publish, at the resolution it was rendered.
  • Full copyright on every image. It is your photo of your client’s property; the output is yours.
  • Eight room types: living room, bedroom, dining room, kitchen, bathroom, office, outdoors, and a Dorm mode that keeps university-issued furniture where it is.
  • Eight furniture styles: Standard, Modern, Midcentury, Scandinavian, Luxury, Coastal, Farmhouse, and Custom, plus a free-text box for the specific request (“keep the room bright, no dark wood”).
  • A gallery that keeps your ten most recent rooms, each stored with the settings that produced it, so you can see what you asked for six listings ago.
  • The “Virtually staged” disclosure stamp, which the next section covers in full.
  • About eight seconds for most images.

And plainly, what it does not include: the higher-quality image model, removing furniture that is already in the room, multiple variations of one render, uploading a photo of a specific sofa to match, gallery search, and the three precision tools (the masking tool, the Masking Studio and the Exterior Studio), along with the AI Designer. Those are Stagify+. We come back to them at the end.

The free feature nobody else has: the disclosure stamp

Every MLS that permits virtual staging, which is effectively all of them, permits it on the condition that you disclose it. We wrote the long version of that in Is Virtual Staging Allowed on the MLS?, including sample wording. The short version: the obligation lands on the listing agent, and it does not go away because the software was free.

So there is a checkbox in the staging panel labelled Label as virtually staged. Tick it and a small “Virtually staged” note is rendered into the bottom-right of the finished photo. Three things about it are deliberate:

  • It is part of the image, not part of our website. A caption you type into a portal field lives in that portal. This travels with the file: into an email, a PDF brochure, a social post, a client’s phone.
  • It is a tag, not a watermark. Four styles (dark, light, minimal, and a full-width banner across the foot of the frame) and a size slider, with a live preview rendered by the same code that renders the final image, so what you approve is what you get. There is a hard ceiling on how large it can go, because a disclosure that dominates the photo is a different problem.
  • It is on every plan, including free. Not an upsell, not a Plus feature, not a “remove branding” toggle inverted into a compliance tool. A legal disclosure that costs $11.99 a month is a bad idea on its own terms.

It is also localised into all eleven languages the site supports, because the stamp is burned into pixels that a non-English-speaking seller may hand to a non-English-speaking buyer, and English there would be the one place the disclosure fails to disclose.

What it does not do is your whole compliance job. It is the identification: two words on the image saying this was staged. Most MLSs also want a line in the listing remarks, and some jurisdictions now want more than a label: California’s AB 723, in force since January 1, 2026, requires that a digitally altered listing image carry both a statement that it was altered and a link, URL or QR code pointing to the original, unaltered photo. Keep your originals, and check your own MLS’s photo policy: we go through every state’s position, and what the MLSs actually require, in the 2026 state-by-state disclosure guide.

Staging a listing for free, start to finish

The tool is the easy part. The photograph is where free results are won or lost, so most of this list is about the shot.

  1. Shoot the room, not the corner. Stand back, keep the camera at eye level, roughly the height a buyer will stand at, and include the floor. The AI places furniture on the floor it can see; give it more floor and it has more to work with.
  2. Resist the ultra-wide lens. This is the single most common cause of odd-looking AI staging. A very wide or fisheye frame bends the vertical lines and the perspective, and furniture placed into a bent room looks placed. A moderate wide angle beats a dramatic one every time.
  3. Use flat, even daylight. Mid-morning with the curtains open. Hard shadows and blown-out windows both cost you detail the model needs to read the space.
  4. Clear the surfaces. If the room still has a few things in it, take them out physically where you can. On the free plan the tool furnishes a room rather than emptying it first, so the emptier the start, the cleaner the result.
  5. Upload. JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 25 MB. iPhone HEIC files are converted in your browser before they are sent, so you can drop them straight in.
  6. Pick the room type and a style, then add one specific sentence in the prompt box if you have a preference. One clear instruction beats five vague ones.
  7. Tick “Label as virtually staged” and pick a stamp style that suits the photo: light on a dark room, dark on a bright one.
  8. Download, then disclose again in the remarks. The stamp is on the image; the sentence goes in the listing.

One thing worth knowing before you upload: a check runs on the photo first and will decline things that are not a property or a piece of furniture: portraits, pets, food, screenshots, documents, vehicles. It is not being difficult. It is refusing to spend a render on an image that cannot produce a useful one, and it tells you why rather than handing back something strange.

When free stops being enough

Honestly: free covers the common case, which is an empty or nearly empty room that needs furnishing. It stops covering you at three specific points.

  • The room is already furnished. Tenanted properties, estate sales, sellers still living there. Removing existing furniture is a harder operation than adding it and it is a Stagify+ feature.
  • You need exact control. Swap one sofa and leave the rest of the shot untouched, or stage four areas of an open-plan space differently in one pass. That is the masking tool and the Masking Studio, where everything outside your highlights stays pixel-for-pixel identical.
  • The photo is of the outside. The staging tools deliberately never touch the exterior; the Exterior Studio handles time of day, sky, and cars and bins in the frame, without altering the property itself.

Stagify+ is $11.99 a month with a seven-day free trial, and adds those three plus the higher-quality image model, multiple variations, furniture reference photos, gallery search and an unlimited gallery. For most agents the useful sequence is to run the free plan across a real listing first, find out which of the three walls you actually hit, and decide then.

The bottom line

“Free” is not a feature. Downloadable, unwatermarked, full-resolution, yours, and labelled. That is a feature, and it is a short enough list to check before you invest an afternoon in a tool.

Run the five questions on us too. That is rather the point of writing them down.

Sources & notes

  • California Legislature, AB 723: Real estate: digitally altered images: disclosure (adds Business and Professions Code § 10140.8)
  • NAR: Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice, Article 12 (truthfulness in advertising)
  • Per-photo and physical staging cost ranges are covered, with sources, in Stagify vs. Other Virtual Staging Tools rather than repeated here. The $16 to $75 per-photo figure on this article’s cover image is that piece’s sourced range.
  • The three free-tier gates described above are general patterns across the category, not claims about any specific named product; free tiers change without notice, which is exactly why the five-question test is written to be run yourself.

cta.body: Unlimited free generations, no watermark, full copyright, and the “Virtually staged” label included on every plan. Upload a photo and see the room furnished in about eight seconds.

english.disclaimer: This article is for general informational purposes only and is not legal advice. Plan features and limits described here reflect Stagify.ai at the time of writing and may change; see the pricing page for current details. Descriptions of other tools’ free tiers are general category patterns rather than statements about any specific product, and such offers change frequently. Disclosure obligations for virtually staged and digitally altered listing photographs vary by MLS, state and jurisdiction and are summarised rather than quoted here; always check your own MLS’s photo and advertising policy and your state real estate commission’s guidance, and disclose edited and virtually staged listing photos accordingly.
